articles.title: Parental Closeness, Communication Quality, and Psychological Adjustment Among Emerging Adult Undergraduates: A Secondary Analysis of the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study
articles.abstract: Emerging adulthood is a developmental period characterized by increasing independence, changing responsibilities, and adjustments in family relationships. Although young adults gain greater autonomy, relationships with parents remain relevant to their emotional well-being and psychological adjustment. Understanding how parental closeness and communication quality relate to these outcomes is especially important among undergraduate students navigating the transition into adult roles. This exploratory secondary analysis examined associations between perceived parental relationship quality, life satisfaction, and depression screening using Year 22 data (2020-2024) from the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study (FFCWS). Of 4,898 cohort records, 726 met the undergraduate eligibility criteria, including 523 with positive national survey weights. Survey-weighted logistic regression models examined maternal and paternal relationship quality while adjusting for age and degree type. National-weighted analyses found no statistically significant associations between parental relationship quality and binary life satisfaction. However, higher maternal relationship quality was associated with lower odds of a positive depression screen (OR = 0.58, 95% CI [0.34, 0.98]). Supplementary unweighted analyses indicated that communication quality was associated with greater life satisfaction independently of perceived closeness. These findings highlight the relevance of parent-young adult relationships to psychological adjustment while suggesting that distinct relationship characteristics may be associated with different outcomes.

articles.title: Society and the Politics of Social (In)Visibilization
articles.abstract: In previous articles I have suggested that the neoliberal age has seen the formation of a new social order whose practices and structures of social (in)visibilization are expanding worldwide, becoming fundamental components of contemporary society. I refer to this rising social order as “the (in)visibilization society.” In this article, I aim to complement part of the theoretical foundations of this sociological concept of society by focusing on what I call "the politics of social (in)visibilization," particularly their spaces and means. With this approach I seek to advance in sketching out a sociological analysis on contemporary societies that addresses a new scenario for both the struggles for social justice and societies more broadly.

articles.title: Terms and Conditions Apply: Citizen-Driven Scenarios on Data Center Construction, Public Values and Acts of Resistance
articles.authors: Kimon Kieslich, Sophie Morosoli, Natali Helberger, Nicholas Diakopoulos
articles.abstract: The massive expansion of AI requires infrastructure development. Governments and tech companies are investing heavily in the construction of large-scale data centers to meet the needs of the tech industry. Data centers consume resources such as energy and water and produce undesirable noise and heat in the process of providing their services. This makes them a subject of public debate, as they can directly impact citizens’ lives. However, the current debate is dominated by top-down visions of AI expansion, in which data centers are seen as an inevitable necessity for competing in the global “AI race”. Much less attention is paid to the communities directly affected by the construction of such infrastructure. In this paper, we explore citizens' visions for their role and agency, including acts of resistance, in decisions around data center construction. To elicit German citizens’ (N=119) imaginations about a future with – or without – data centers, we used scenario-writing as a method, a future-thinking approach in which respondents are tasked with writing short normative stories about plausible future developments. Additionally, we asked respondents to reflect on their own agency in this process, i.e. how they might influence such data center construction. Our qualitative thematic analysis identifies themes relating to future trajectories, as well as patterns of resistance to AI, as articulated by citizens. Our study contributes to the emerging debate around data center construction by adding a public opinion angle that is grounded in conceptual thoughts of public values and AI resistance.

articles.title: PARTYPRESS: A Sentence-Level Database of Party Issue Attention using Press Releases from 29 European Democracies from 2010 to 2026
articles.abstract: The issues parties emphasise between elections remain understudied compared to the study of election manifestos. We introduce a comparative database of parties’ press releases containing 650,367 releases by 160 parties in 29 European democracies between 2010 and 2026. Parties’ near-daily statements cover issue attention between elections, responses to events, and which issues are raised alongside each other. All 8.5 million sentences receive a topic code, validated against native-speaker hand coding. Coding sentences rather than whole releases gives each issue’s share of a release, yields more reliable party time series, and shows which issues appear alongside each other. We demonstrate the value of this approach by examining how parties responded to the 2021–22 energy crisis. Parties’ energy communication surged, mostly in releases that did not address climate – a shift that document-level coding cannot reveal. Party series at three resolutions and a web explorer make the data readily usable without code.

articles.title: Network Externalities, Community Structure, and Inequality in Migration Diffusion: Evidence From Mexico-U.S. Migration, 1965–2018
articles.abstract: Why do migration flows grow and persist in some communities but stall or remain modest in others? We argue that the answer lies in the interplay between network externalities and community social structure. Following DiMaggio and Garip, we treat migration as a practice with positive network externalities: as more community members migrate, the costs of migration fall for those who remain, generating a self-reinforcing dynamic in which past migration begets future migration. Yet whether these externalities produce broadly shared or narrowly concentrated migration opportunities depends on two structural properties of the sending community: homophily (proxied by the homogeneity of socioeconomic traits) and consolidation (the degree to which socioeconomic traits are intercorrelated). We hypothesize that high homophily and high consolidation constrain network externalities within narrow social clusters, limiting the reach of cumulative causation and concentrating migration gains among those already well-positioned to migrate. We test these predictions using longitudinal individual-level data from 151 Mexican communities observed between 1965 and 2018. Our results confirm that migration prevalence, a community-level proxy for accumulated network externalities, is positively associated with new migration. This relationship, however, peaks earlier and saturates more quickly in communities where socioeconomic traits are more homogeneous and highly intercorrelated. We discuss implications for theories of cumulative causation and migration inequality.

articles.title: Before the answer is published: testing AI hypothesis generation against a sealed study
articles.abstract: Claims that AI systems can generate research hypotheses are rarely tested against an answer the model cannot already know. Evaluations that score hypotheses against papers published after a model’s training cutoff lose that protection with each new model. This article proposes a protocol that uses as its answer key an empirical study that has never been published, sealed by its author and committed only as a hash before any generation. Around the key, the protocol combines a time-cut literature corpus, a frozen preregistration, a same-model restatement baseline that separates proposing from paraphrasing prior findings, scoring blind to group and a scripted verdict, each recorded as a separate commit. The protocol was run twice on an unpublished doctoral study in economic geography with five findings. In the preregistered run, the main model scored no higher when proposing than when restating high-cite prior studies (1.5 versus 1.5 of 5), and no hypothesis recovered any finding in full. The run’s records traced this floor in part to two design failures that recur easily in such evaluations: a one-sentence hypothesis template and a safeguard that left retrieval unvaried. An exploratory second run fixed both. Proposing then beat restating for the main model (0.83 versus 0.23 per output; difference 0.60, 95% interval 0.47 to 0.72) but not for an open-weight model trained before the corpus cutoff (difference 0.05), and again no output recovered a finding in full. Because the gain appears only in the model that may have been exposed to later literature and to the study itself, it cannot be read as capability. Both runs are reported as tests of the protocol, failures included.

articles.title: Towards Inclusive Landscape Governance: A Dialogue between Indigenous, Local and Western Academic Knowledges.
articles.authors: Onintsoa Ravaka Andriamihaja, Krystal Bedregal, Meredith Cristina Castro Rios, Tabea Casique Coronado, Julio Ricardo Cusurichi Palacios, Gabriela Gonzales Malca, David Hecht, Zsófia Szonja Illés, Yesica Patiachi Tayori, Anjaratiana Rojo Rasamoelina
articles.abstract: Landscape governance has emerged to address global concerns such as biodiversity loss, climate change, and unsustainable resource use. Central to this endeavor is the inclusion of Indigenous and local knowledges (ILK), which are often marginalized in favor of Western academic knowledges (WAK) reflecting unequal power relations in the recognition and legitimacy of different knowledge systems. This article explores how different types of knowledge contribute to inclusive landscape governance through a multi-case, participatory and self-reflective approach grounded in knowledge dialogues in diverse case study landscapes. The results highlight a broad range of knowledge types, including ILK, WAK, and hybrid forms. ILK was found to be grounded in specific cultural, linguistic, and territorial contexts, while hybrid practices combined experiential and scientific insights. Knowledge use was diverse and multifaceted, supporting land and resource management, cultural preservation, and environmental sustainability. Knowledge was preserved through oral traditions, ritual practices, and digital repositories, and transmitted across generations and communities through storytelling, arts, and participatory methods. The article underscores that knowledge for landscape governance is not static content but a situated, relational, and evolving practice. ILK plays a central role in shaping landscapes and strengthening adaptive capacity, yet it remains undervalued in formal governance frameworks. More inclusive and dialogic approaches, rooted in epistemic justice, pluralism, and Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC), are required to move beyond consultation toward an inclusive landscape governance. By examining how different knowledge systems are recognised, negotiated, and mobilised, this article contributes to political ecology debates on knowledge, power, and human–environment relationships.

articles.title: Sustainable Public Sports Facility Management in Malawi: A Scoping Review of Global and Sub-Saharan African Evidence

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Background: Sustainability has become a central concern in sports facility management, yet research remains concentrated in high-income countries, and the evidence base for Sub-Saharan Africa, including Malawi, has not been systematically mapped. Objective: To map the global, regional and Malawi-specific literature on sustainable public sports facility management, synthesise it through the Triple Bottom Line (TBL) framework and identify priority research gaps. Methods: The review followed the Arksey and O’Malley (2005) framework, as refined by Levac et al. (2010), and is reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR (Tricco et al., 2018). OpenAlex and Lens.org were searched without date restriction (retrieved records spanned 2008–2026), supplemented by Google Scholar, reference-list searching and targeted grey-literature searching. Records were screened against predefined eligibility criteria, and included sources were charted by geographic scope, TBL pillar and source type. Results: Fifty-two sources were included on the basis of title and abstract screening. Global research emphasises technology-led and corporate social responsibility (CSR)-driven sustainability in resource-rich contexts. Sub-Saharan African research is sparse, clustered around South Africa’s hosting of the 2010 FIFA World Cup, and dominated by maintenance-management and institutional-capacity studies rather than empirical evaluation of sustainability interventions. Malawi-specific evidence consists of one peer-reviewed study and a small body of institutional and media reports; no Malawi-specific source was retrieved through the primary database searches. Conclusions: Five priority gaps were identified: contextual adaptation of TBL to low-resource public facilities; empirical evidence linking community engagement to reduced vandalism and related risks; sport-specific, rather than general, infrastructure research; integrated cross-pillar assessment tools; and longitudinal data on facility deterioration. Together, these gaps define a research agenda for scholars and a planning reference for facility managers and policymakers in Sub-Saharan Africa. Keywords: sustainable facility management; sports facilities; Triple Bottom Line; Sub-Saharan Africa; Malawi; scoping review; community engagement

articles.title: Can Public Dissociation Protect Environmental Organizations from Radical Flank Violence?
articles.abstract: What can nonviolent organizations do—or say—when violence committed by radicals on their movement's fringes threatens their public standing? I examine one possible strategy, public dissociation, through which nonviolent organizations distinguish themselves from violence committed in the name of their cause or those responsible for it. I argue that such statements can limit the reputational costs organizations might otherwise incur from violence in which they played no part. I test this argument in two preregistered survey experiments involving 3,000 U.S. respondents, using scenarios in which an environmental organization confronts eco-sabotage by an ideologically adjacent radical group. I find that public dissociation increases support for the nonviolent organization relative to silence, although the reputational costs of silence vary across dimensions of public support. These findings suggest a more complex understanding of the reputational consequences of political violence, in which nonviolent actors can influence how violence committed by others affects their public standing.

articles.title: WIDE Data Analysis: enabling wide, detailed and interactive data practice
articles.authors: Roger Beecham, Cagatay Turkay, Jo Wood, Levi Wolf, Rachel S. Franklin, Daniel Archambault, Benjamin Bach, Dianne Cook, Andrew Gelman, Jessica Hullman
articles.abstract: In data analysis there is a tension between perceived methodological rigour and analytic richness. While formally pre-stated analysis protocols may confer ‘rigour’, through repeatable (and automatable) plans, in locking-down the data analysis process they may risk important phenomena being missed, or alternative perspectives being overlooked. We present WIDE Data Analysis to improve the balance with which data analysis is conducted. Our proposal consists of four strategies – [w]idening, [i]nteracting, [d]etailing and [e]nabling – and accompanying qualities or values that a successful data analysis should attain – replication value, didactic value, generative value, ludic/play value. We explain how critical data practices such as sensitivity analysis, many-model thinking, visual data analysis and storytelling underpin these strategies and values. Inspired by D’Ignazio and Klein’s data feminism (2020), we then develop prompting questions that compel analysts to reflect on the key decision points of an analysis, and envisage how these prompting questions, together with the critical data practices, might be called upon in AI-backed computational notebook environments. Our thesis is that at a moment when large parts of data analysis are being automated, frameworks such as WIDE that eschew a recipe-based approach to science are urgently needed.

articles.title: Fiscal Accountability or Regime Shift? Machine Learning and Causal Evidence from Philippine Gubernatorial Elections (1992–2022)
articles.abstract: Do voters reward governors for better health and education spending, increased local revenue, and lower dependence on intergovernmental transfers? This question lies at the heart of whether fiscal devolution under the 1991 Local Government Code has actually strengthened democratic accountability at the subnational level. Using a panel of Philippine provinces (1992–2022) and an XGBoost classifier, we find that while the model achieves 95.5% cross-validated accuracy under random splitting, this is an artefact of panel leakage. When evaluated with grouped cross-validation that holds out entire provinces, accuracy falls to 50.4%, barely above random guessing. Rolling-window temporal validation confirms that the model fails to generalise across any period (37–57%). The high within-sample accuracy is not evidence of a stable fiscal-electoral relationship; rather, both cross-sectional leakage and temporal non-stationarity contribute to the model's generalisation failure. The post-2016 period shows no systematic deterioration beyond the model's baseline inability to generalise; performance is consistently near or below chance across all out-of-sample years. SHAP analysis identifies the interaction between dynasty status and IRA dependence as the most important predictor in the non-generalising model, though this ranking shifts substantially over time. A regression discontinuity design, estimated on two-candidate gubernatorial races to correctly account for plurality elections, finds that winning a close election increases subsequent health spending growth by 0.56–0.73 percentage points (ATE = 0.564, 95% CI [0.072, 1.057] at optimal bandwidth). We conclude that predictive models of electoral accountability require both grouped cross-validation and temporal validation as minimum standards of rigour, and that fiscal-electoral relationships are neither cross-sectionally generalisable nor temporally stable.

articles.title: How causal are published QCA solutions? Bounding the probabilities of causation behind configurational findings
articles.abstract: Qualitative Comparative Analysis (QCA) reports sufficiency paths with consistency and coverage, and applied articles often read each path as a causal recipe. Crisp consistency is the outcome frequency inside a path and never uses the outcome frequency outside it. We ask which causal claim published solutions can support once translated into Pearl's probabilities of necessity (PN), sufficiency (PS), and necessity and sufficiency (PNS). Following a written protocol fixed before the audit, CB-QCA replicates published solutions from open data and bounds these quantities for every path and complete solution. Of 92 unique studies attempted, 43 replicated exactly (17 crisp-set, 26 fuzzy-set), giving 282 paths and 68 solutions; fuzzy-set memberships are dichotomised at 0.5. Under exogeneity, the data guarantee PS ≥ 0.5 for every crisp-set path, while the data and exogeneity do not guarantee it for 40 of 181 fuzzy-set paths (22 %). The exact 95 % per-term sampling bound is uninformative for 76 % of paths and 28 % of complete solutions; among paths with five or fewer cases, a one-sided Fisher test reaches p < 0.05 for only 9 %. We recommend reporting cases per path, the outcome frequency outside it, and an exact sampling bound.

articles.title: THE GOLD CONTENT OF THE SOVIET RUBLE IN THE 1920s–1940s: THE EVOLUTION OF OFFICIAL PARITY AND ACTUAL VALUE
articles.abstract: The article examines the relationship between the official gold parity of the Soviet ruble and its actual value in the 1920s–1940s. It systematizes the available source base, which includes departmental document collections, Western diplomatic and financial materials, and archival data on domestic gold prices and the purchasing power of the ruble, and notes that much of the Soviet archival material remains inaccessible. Normative values and exchange rates are used to calculate the theoretical gold equivalents of the ruble. Under the 1922–1924 reform it stood at 0.774234 g, in 1936 at 0.176850 g, and after the rate of 5.30 rubles per dollar was introduced in 1937 at 0.167674 g. From 1 March 1950 a new value of 0.222168 g was formally established. The study finds that the decline in the equivalent in 1936–1937 was not accompanied by a legal definition of a new gold content, and that the 1947 monetary reform left the parity unchanged. A comparison with the multiple gold prices (from 5.91 to 44.57 rubles per gram in 1949), the cost of gold mining, and the ruble–dollar ratios for commodities shows that the formal stability of the exchange rate in 1937–1949 coincided with a widening gap between the official and the economic value of the currency.

articles.title: Housing Affordability and Commuting Patterns in Central Texas: A County-Level Analysis, 2015-2024

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: This study investigates the shifts in terms of housing affordability and commuting in the five counties in Central Texas: Bastrop, Caldwell, Hays, Travis, and Williamson. The comparison is done based on the 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 periods according to American Community Survey (ACS) five-year estimates. Datasets B08303 (Travel Time to Work) and B25106 (Tenure by Housing Costs as a Percentage of Household Income) are utilized for the calculations of the percentage of employees who commute for 30 minutes or more and the percentage of rental households that spend 30% or more of their income on gross rent. All calculations have been performed using Python. Results showed that long commutes were observed to increase in three counties, while renter cost burden increased in three counties and decreased in two. Long commutes and renter cost burdens increased in Hays County; however, long commutes increased while renter cost burden decreased in Bastrop and Caldwell counties. The correlation results indicate that there was a more negative relationship between the variables in the latter period. However, the small number of five counties makes the conclusion difficult. Overall, the findings highlight differences in housing affordability and commuting patterns across Central Texas and the importance of considering both in regional planning.

articles.title: Disentangling Cultural Likert Response Styles, Multi-Informant Discrepancy Polarity, and Institutional Support Regimes Across Four Anglophone K–12 Systems: A Coordinated Integrative Data Analysis of 2,280 Families
articles.abstract: Cross-national K–12 comparisons across Anglophone systems routinely equate scalar invariance with unbiased observed scores, overlooking culturally patterned Likert scale usage, domain-specific parent–youth discrepancy reversals, and heterogeneity within pooled Commonwealth samples. Using coordinated Integrative Data Analysis (IDA) across four Wave 1 cohorts—burnout (HABRI), parenting (HPSSI), executive functioning (HEFSI), and self-regulated learning (HSRLI)—this study analyzed 311,840 ordinal responses from N = 2,280 families (1,618 Grades 4–12 dyads and 662 Grades K–3 parents in the United States [n = 1,377], United Kingdom [n = 580], Canada [n = 279], and Australia/Other Commonwealth [n = 44]) plus J = 480 Core-60 Differential Item Functioning (DIF) parameters. Multi-process IRTree models revealed monotonic U.S.-to-Commonwealth shifts from extreme (F[3, 2276] = 22.81, p < .001) to midpoint responding (F[3, 2276] = 18.53, p < .001) and strong household concordance (r = .749–.792); purifying response styles eliminated apparent U.S. executive-function leads while sharpening Canadian and British burnout elevations. Directional parent–youth discrepancies inverted polarity between burnout and home safety (F[9, 1599] = 2.40, p = .011), British profile agreement dipped at ages 9–11 (p = .011), and recreational screen time interacted with national special-education support (F[3, 1604] = 6.20, p < .001). Open-access multi-language instrument forms, scoring documentation, baseline invariance summary matrices (N = 3,809), and copyright-holder adaptation permissions (ITC Guideline PC-1) are archived at https://openinventories.org.

articles.title: Air Pollution and the A-H Premium: Pre-Registered Evidence from Shanghai–Hong Kong Dual Listings and the Limits of Meteorological Instruments
articles.abstract: Two published studies report that air pollution moves the price gap between the Shanghai (A) and Hong Kong (H) listings of the same Chinese firm, and attribute it to different behavioural channels. Because the two listings carry identical cash-flow rights but trade to investor populations of which only one breathes Shanghai air, the sign of the response separates mood (negative), cognitive impairment (positive) and a response common to both populations (zero). Instrumenting daily Shanghai PM2.5 with dispersion conditions (effective F 107) across 61 pairs and 64,422 firm-days from 2014 to 2019, a one standard deviation rise in log PM2.5 moves the premium by 0.73 basis points (95% Anderson-Rubin set −15.5 to +18.1). A pre-registered equivalence test rejects effects larger than 25 basis points, and placebo cities with strong first stages of their own show nothing. Winter-only estimates are positive but rest on the instrument's weakest season. The same instruments fail for Hong Kong, where the reanalysis boundary layer is wrong-signed in winter because the northeast monsoon brings pollution on well-mixed days, on our reading of the seasonal pattern. An exploratory screen of 365 Chinese cities finds such inversions in 22, almost all south of 28°N, so dispersion instruments need a seasonal sign check.

articles.title: Comparing the effects of three economic crises on U.S. household finances
articles.abstract: Economic crises put pressure on family budgets through increased costs and unemployment, but it is unclear whether households suffered larger losses from specific sources in recent U.S. crises and who suffered most. This study examined the impacts of the 2007-2009 Global Financial Crisis (GFC), the COVID recession, and the post-pandemic inflation period on U.S. families, and whether government responses reduced their losses. It was hypothesized that unemployment would generate the biggest losses in the GFC and COVID and consumer prices during the inflation period. Using a cash-flow model for four representative households built from federal surveys, each crisis was compared with pre-crisis trends, and this was repeated for 2,000 runs. Supporting the hypothesis, unemployment generated the biggest losses in all runs in the GFC and COVID, and a type of consumer price did so in 80-100% of runs during the inflation period. Without government payments, a lower-income renter family lost 5.3% of annual income in COVID. When one worker lost a job, lower-income families lost 9.7-13.9% and used up all savings in every crisis. Government payments helped in most recession scenarios, but no broad payment was made during the inflation period. Losses also depended on the baseline and wage measure, but the main source of loss did not change across the 2,000 runs. The results suggest lower-income families with little savings are most vulnerable in every crisis.

articles.title: Policy brief: Protection of Indonesian students and citizens in Turkey: challenges and recommendations

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Indonesian students in Turkey who convert rupiah into Turkish lira frequently rely on exchange services offered by fellow members of the diaspora. This arrangement fills a real gap left by formal banking, yet it also exposes students to fraud, and victims seldom seek legal remedy because they distrust institutions and know little about Turkish law. Drawing on the author’s four years of study in Turkey and on peer-reviewed research about international students, informal value transfer, migrants’ trust in law enforcement, and legal literacy, this policy brief examines why fraud in informal currency exchange persists and how Indonesian and Turkish authorities can respond. It compares four courses of action and recommends a combined package: a criteria-based verification service with a secure transaction platform, legal-literacy and reporting support developed with student associations, and a coordination channel with Turkish authorities, with an official low-cost exchange channel as a medium-term goal. The brief also assesses the main risks, including the legal feasibility of the proposed rehabilitation period, and identifies where evidence from Turkey is still missing.

articles.title: Cartographic Knowledge: Redefining Knowledge in Light of Evolutionary Theory — An Anthropological Study
articles.abstract: Forms of knowledge with no direct link to survival—religious knowledge foremost among them—have long posed a challenge to evolutionary theory: the cost of belief in unseen deities is difficult to justify under natural selection, in the way that the cost of three-dimensional vision is not. This study locates the source of the difficulty in an epistemological assumption inherited from classical philosophy: that consciousness produces knowledge as a correspondence to reality, and therefore that some knowledge lies beyond the function of survival. Against this, it proposes the concept of "cartographic knowledge": consciousness is a multi-mechanism adaptive apparatus whose function is not to mirror reality but to draw a functional map of the environment, material and symbolic, by which the organism selects survival enhancing behavior. On this view, all knowledge, religious and non-religious alike, is map data generated within a single function; and since every representation is built from sense derived primitives, the religious image is not the reception of transcendent data but a recombination of sensed elements extrapolated beyond the sensed. The framework is offered as falsifiable, and it unifies otherwise scattered evolutionary accounts of religion — hypersensitive agency detection, theory of mind, and cultural evolution — within a single cartographic process. Its contribution is to reinsert every category of knowledge into the logic of evolution.

articles.title: Rehearse Before You Travel: A Conceptual Model of AI-Assisted Travel Rehearsal and the Self-Fading AI Hypothesis

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Tourists abroad routinely face short, consequential service encounters: an inflated taxi fare, a pharmacy visit in an unfamiliar language, a room that does not match the booking. Research on generative artificial intelligence (AI) in tourism has concentrated on how such systems help travellers plan, choose and delegate decisions, and on how AI support during a trip shapes confidence and satisfaction. Separately, research in language education, health-professions education and workplace training shows that rehearsal with simulated counterparts can build skills, although transfer of those skills to real settings is conditional rather than automatic. This conceptual article brings these streams together for the tourist. It proposes the AI-Assisted Travel Rehearsal (ATR) model, an iterative cycle in which travellers rehearse anticipated encounters with general-purpose conversational AI before and during a trip, receive minimal AI support in real encounters, and reflect on each encounter to plan the next rehearsal. Drawing on social cognitive theory, experiential learning theory, the transactional model of stress and coping, scaffolding and fading, and transfer-of-training research, the article specifies a mechanism linking rehearsal to mastery experience, situational self-efficacy and behavioural capability, conditional transfer, and progressive AI fading. Its central claim, the Self-Fading AI Hypothesis, holds that well-designed AI support should reduce travellers' reliance on AI in real encounters without loss of independent performance; reduced AI use alone is not treated as evidence of autonomy. The article states six propositions with explicit conditions of support, identifies which can be tested confirmatorily, and proposes a randomised, actively controlled classroom experiment with AI-unavailable and AI-available transfer tasks, followed by a multilevel field study of first-time international travellers. No empirical results are reported.

articles.title: The data center next door: Feared and realized effects on home values in the Seoul metropolitan area, South Korea
articles.abstract: Residents who oppose data centers near their homes fear a loss of home value. Existing estimates, such as a 7% decline within one mile of U.S. data-center campuses, may not apply to buildings among apartment blocks in a dense city. To test whether prices fall there, I compare complexes within 500 m of 24 data centers permitted in the Seoul metropolitan area of South Korea in 2017–2025 with complexes 1–2 km away, before and after the building permit, using 205,000 sales and 287,000 lump-sum (jeonse) leases. Sale prices show no decline distinguishable from zero after the permit (0.0%; 95% CI −1.6% to 1.6%), and tenants' deposits were unchanged through the first two years of operation. Estimates across control groups and samples range from −1.6% to 0.5%, and all rule out a 7% loss. Evaluations of siting rules in dense cities should not assume the losses measured around U.S. campuses.

articles.title: Imported Rates, Domestic Risk: Global Saving–Investment Shifts and the Exposure of Canadian REITs
articles.abstract: Canadian real estate investment trusts (REITs) hold buildings that last for decades and pay for them largely with debt that has to be rolled over again and again. That makes them far more exposed to long-term interest rates than to the overnight rate the Bank of Canada sets. In this paper I review what economists and real estate researchers have found on three questions: (i) what sets long-term real interest rates, (ii) how Canadian yields take on those global forces, and (iii) how long-term rates feed through to REIT refinancing costs, property values, tenant demand, and balance-sheet limits. The macro literature agrees that real rates fell for four decades; it does not agree on whether they will rise again. I argue that, on balance, the evidence points to a higher equilibrium than in the 2010s. Saving is weakening (an ageing population, large fiscal deficits, China’s rebalancing) while demand for investment is growing (AI infrastructure, the energy transition, emerging-market growth). Secular stagnation remains the main case against this view. The real estate literature supports four transmission channels but says little, at the level of the firm, about how they interact. I then use Allied Properties REIT’s 2026 reporting as an illustrative case to see which channels have actually been at work. So far, higher rates have shown up mainly in valuations (nine-month fair value losses of $932 million, with capitalization and discount rates up 36 to 49 basis points) and in leverage ratios. Most of the higher refinancing cost is still ahead, and a substantial share of the stress comes from factors that have little to do with rates. I close with implications for REIT management and an agenda for further research.

articles.title: Holistic Parenting & Student Support Inventory (HPSSI): Multi-Informant Psychometric Validation, Incremental Validity, and COSMIN Two-Week Test–Retest Reliability Across Grades K–12
articles.abstract: Why do legacy parenting scales miss modern family friction? Questionnaires such as the Alabama Parenting Questionnaire (APQ) predated smartphones, online gaming, and school portals, and rarely supply equated parent and youth forms across Grades K–12. This two-wave study validates the Holistic Parenting & Student Support Inventory (HPSSI) across a 60-item clinical battery (Core-60; eight subscales spanning Relational Climate, Digital Mediation & Screen Regulation, and Academic & School Alignment) and a nested 40-item screener (Short-40). Subject-matter experts (N = 28; Core-60 polarity-adjusted S-CVI/Ave = .846) and cognitive-probing dyads (N = 16; ICI = .969) verified content clarity. In Wave 1 (N = 659 K–12 families: 440 Grades 4–12 dyads and 219 Grades K–3 parents across the U.S., U.K., Canada, and Australia), ordinal WLSMV CFA supported the eight-factor model (Core-60 CFI = .953–.968, RMSEA = .048–.051; Short-40 CFI = .958–.973), high reliability (ωt = .954–.966), dyadic concordance (r = .773), and scalar invariance across informant, sex, and grade band. Dyadic scores explained incremental variance beyond all five APQ scales across 11 criteria (ΔR2 = +.085 to +.204, p < .001). Wave 2 (~14 days; N = 203 clean dyads; U.S. n = 122 ≥ 100) confirmed temporal stability: Parent ICC(2,1) = .814 [.756, .858] (SEM = 0.20, MDC95 = 0.56); Student ICC(2,1) = .792 [.733, .838] (SEM = 0.25, MDC95 = 0.70). Open-access multi-language instrument forms, scoring documentation, baseline invariance summary matrices (N = 3,809), and copyright-holder adaptation permissions (ITC Guideline PC-1) are archived at https://openinventories.org.

articles.title: Distinct but Inseparable: Mental Health as Cognitive-Security Infrastructure

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Cognitive-security discourse increasingly treats attention, judgment, belief, and decision-making as strategic terrain. This conceptual position paper argues that mental health and well-being are cognitive-security infrastructure: autonomous cognition depends on allostatic, affective, relational, moral, social, and environmental conditions that mental-health sciences already study and support. Psychoneuroimmunology provides the biological bridge; allostasis and allostatic load explain how adaptive stress can become cumulative burden; Operator Syndrome provides a sentinel case; and cyberpsychology, digitally extended cognition, liminal warfare, the Fog of Living, thoughtforms, and Cognitive Aikido extend the argument into contemporary cognitive-warfare environments. Existing clinical modalities and psychometric tools are treated as a capability library rather than as technologies to be repackaged under new security terminology. Disaster behavioral health, Anticipate, Plan, and Deter, and PsySTART® provide an operational model for exposure-based triage and recovery. The paper situates NATO cognitive-warfare doctrine and documented Chinese and Russian influence strategies within a politically agnostic human-impact framework focused on suffering, agency, belief, emotional contagion, social trust, and recovery. It concludes that cognitive security should make the mental-health ecosystem a core partner from threat modeling through recovery, under an addition-without-subtraction principle that expands capability without displacing clinical science, workforce, ethics, or care infrastructure. Keywords: cognitive security, mental health, allostatic load, psychoneuroimmunology, cognitive resilience, disaster behavioral health, agency, belief

articles.title: SafeConnect AI: A Formative Evaluation of Child Online Safety, Parental Views and Privacy Across 45 Family Dyads
articles.abstract: Children's online interactions increasingly take place across gaming, messaging, social media and educational platforms. Supporting their safety requires more than detecting potentially harmful messages: safety interventions must also be understandable, proportionate and respectful of children's privacy and developing autonomy. This study presents a formative evaluation of SafeConnect AI, a browser-based prototype exploring contextual safety warnings, graduated interventions and parental visibility in child online communication. The study involved 45 parent-child dyads (90 participants) across seven countries. Children were divided into two age groups: 7-11 years (n = 16) and 12-16 years (n = 29). Data were collected between 1 October and 5 November 2026 through supervised online and onsite sessions. Parents evaluated the prototype and its proposed safety features, while children interacted with fictional, age-appropriate scenarios and provided age-adapted feedback. Among parents, 33 of 45 (73.3%) considered real-time alerts useful, 31 (68.9%) preferred explanations accompanying alerts, and 30 (66.7%) favoured graduated interventions. Thirty-six (80.0%) preferred full details in parental safety visibility, while 29 (64.4%) expressed willingness to consider adopting a system of this kind. Thirty-nine (86.7%) reported that the alert logic was clear. However, 20 (44.4%) noticed false alarms during the evaluation, indicating the importance of contextual interpretation and proportionate intervention. Children's responses indicated differences in baseline online safety knowledge and help-seeking confidence between age groups. Post-interaction feedback was generally favourable among younger participants, while older participants expressed more varied views, particularly concerning explanations, intrusiveness and personal control. The findings provide formative evidence about family expectations and the usability considerations involved in designing child-centred online safety support. They do not establish the technical accuracy or real-world effectiveness of an operational AI detection system. The study highlights the need for transparent explanations, age-appropriate interventions, meaningful child agency and privacy-conscious parental oversight.

articles.title: Which deaths count? Mortality shocks from war, famine, and COVID-19 and the attention they receive, 237 countries, 1914–2023
articles.authors: Carlos Alberto Reina Bolaños, Ingrid Liliana Minotta Díaz, Juan Danyster Montoya Cardona

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: COVID-19 was called the largest mortality crisis in generations, yet comparisons with wars, genocides and famines have relied on absolute death counts, which confound severity with population size. Using UN World Population Prospects 2024, we estimated excess mortality and life-expectancy loss for 237 countries and classified national mortality shocks from 1955 to 2023. We compared both world wars with COVID-19 in 15 Human Mortality Database populations and measured PubMed records and humanitarian funding per excess death. The 1959–1961 Chinese famine and COVID-19 caused similar global excess deaths (19.9 vs 15.6 million), but global life expectancy fell 4.9 vs 2.2 years in the worst year. Among 211 classified shocks, the median worst-year loss of life expectancy was 7.6 years for genocide, 5.1 for famine, 4.7 for armed conflict and 2.7 for COVID-19, and the worst First World War year cost belligerent countries 14–21 times more life expectancy than the worst COVID-19 year. Since 2000, COVID-19 received 4 times more publications per death than armed conflict and 16 times more than famine, while humanitarian funding per death declined as severity increased. The crises that cost the most life expectancy receive the least attention per death.

articles.title: Access Before Recruitment: Reaching a Discreet Community in Turkey
articles.abstract: Hard-to-reach communities are usually approached through gatekeepers or referral chains. This retrospective analysis examines a case where most of what preceded and surrounded access took place before recruitment began: how I came to interview 44 home-educating mothers in Turkey, where the practice is unregulated, through a closed online group joined years earlier. Using the doctoral thesis and documents, it reconstructs a sequence of actions and states what cannot be claimed about them. My researcher role became known step by step: to members who asked online, over coffee, at a family camp and in a written statement on joining a second group. Only then did I post a call for participants. A request for referrals produced no names. One interviewee shared my message, and six people who had met me came forward. The time before recruitment deserves reporting as part of access, together with its ethical cost: a period of non-disclosure.

articles.title: State-Level Two-Child Policies and Progression to a Third Child in India: Evidence from Three Policy Waves How Effective are they, and for Whom?

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Over the past few decades, a number of states of India implemented two-child policies as population control measures. Still, two-child policies remain under consideration by states and the nation even as the country's total fertility rate has fallen below replacement with restrictions in some states and recently promises for cash transfers for larger families in others. Whether governments have penalised third births or paid families to have them has depended on political agendas rather than demographic needs.This paper investigates the effectiveness of implemented policies in achieving their intended demographic objectives. Using difference-in-differences analysis with matching techniques on three rounds of National Family Health Survey data (2005-2021), we examine whether these policies reduced progression to a third birth, and whether they did so differently for families without sons and for poor households. Two-child policies produced only a modest additional reduction in third births, concentrated in the 1996 and 2004 waves, and no detectable effect in the most recent 2007 wave. Families without sons were substantially more likely to have a third child than families with at least one son, before the policy and after, in implementation and comparison states alike; the same ordering holds, more weakly, for poor versus non-poor households. Neither differential narrowed after implementation. Triple-difference estimates provide no evidence that the policies operated differently by poverty status in any wave, or by sibling sex composition. This study advances the literature on population policy by showing that son preference and economic constraint structure third-birth behaviour independently of the policy, and that the instruments these policies rely on: disqualification from government employment and from contesting local elections engage in neither. These findings have substantial implications for population policy design in developing countries, suggesting that effective interventions must address underlying socioeconomic determinants and cultural norms rather than relying primarily on incentive structures that conflict with deeply held values and economic realities.

articles.title: Out of Sync at the Table: Habit, Absence, and the Silent Drift of Family Taste
articles.abstract: A homecomer prepares a family dish as they remember making it. The family finds it too sweet, and someone asks why it is being served before New Year. The cook expected a familiar reception. The family expected the cook to know how the dish is now made and when it is served. Why can the discrepancy surprise both sides? This article develops a mechanism linking commensality, habit, and absence. It draws on Schütz's account of homecoming and Etzrodt's reconstruction of habitual action. Shared meals expose participants to one another's responses, so people adjust without repeatedly evaluating the practice as a whole. When shared meals stop, each side continues to make locally intelligible adjustments without discovering how far its expectations have diverged from the other's. The first shared meal at which the dish is served discloses that accumulated discrepancy at once. The argument distinguishes this process from one-sided lag. It specifies which judgments mediated contact can sustain, and it explains how an ordinary habit can become a tradition deliberately maintained. Five propositions identify observations that would strengthen or weaken the account.

articles.title: Antigypsyism in France: Persistent Distance, Distant Empathy
articles.authors: Tommaso Vitale, Yuma Ando, Nonna Mayer, Vincent Tiberj
articles.abstract: Antigypsyism is the most persistent and socially tolerated form of ethnic prejudice in France, yet its structure remains poorly specified. Drawing on the CNCDH Racism Barometer, a nationally representative face-to-face survey conducted in November and December 2025 (N=1,013), this chapter analyzes anti-Roma prejudice toward people of Romani language, most of whom are French citizens. Five attitudinal items (imputed nomadism, child exploitation, theft, refusal to integrate, contested citizenship) form a tightly correlated scale: antigypsyism operates as a coherent representational system, not scattered opinions. Sixty-four percent perceive Roma as a group apart, two and a half to three times the level recorded for other minorities. A blockwise hierarchical logistic regression introduces demographics, social position, territorial context, subjective perceptions, and political orientation in nested steps (pseudo-R² rising from 0.06 to 0.28). Partisan proximity, an index of political polarization, is by far the strongest predictor, ahead of felt economic decline, age, and migratory origin. We argue that antigypsyism is best understood through civic boundary-making (Lamont): a socially organized repertoire activated where local governance and public discourse stage Romani presence as a problem of order, and partially contained where routinized co-presence makes that staging less rewarding. The longitudinal attitude survey also documents a paradox we name distant empathy: memorial recognition of the wartime genocide reaches a record high while present citizenship is still contested by nearly one third. Recognition advances faster in principle than in ordinary neighbourly practice across France.

articles.title: Exploring horizontal homophony in pronominal paradigms: A case study where cross-linguistic regularities defy individual learning biases
articles.abstract: Although number neutralisation—the loss of singular-plural distinctions—is relatively rare in paradigms of personal pronouns, it is the most common pattern of pronominal syncretism cross-linguistically and exhibits systematic asymmetries across person values. Number distinctions are most frequently neutralised in third person, less so in second person, and least often in first person. While this generalisation has been widely noted, its empirical foundation to date remains relatively weak, and no clear mechanistic explanation has been established for why this typological asymmetry might arise. To address this gap, we investigate whether cross-linguistic patterns of number neutralisation might reflect biases in learning, such that patterns that are easier to learn are more reliably transmitted over time and consequently become more prevalent across languages. We first conduct a large-scale synchronic analysis of pronominal paradigms (1,243 languages), confirming a frequency-based hierarchy (3rd > 2nd > 1st) but challenging its previously assumed implicational nature (1st > 2nd > 3rd; i.e., if in 1st, then in 2nd, and if in 2nd, then in 3rd). A diachronic phylogenetic analysis suggests a tendency towards greater stability of number neutralisation in the order 3rd > 2nd > 1st. Overall, however, it provides limited support for the frequency-based hierarchy and no clear support for the implicational hierarchy. Finally, an artificial language learning experiment testing the learnability of different neutralisation patterns reveals that learners do not mirror typological tendencies: contrary to predictions—and in line with an author-based bias—first-person number neutralisation appears to be most learnable. These findings suggest that the typological evidence for the number neutralisation hierarchy might not be as robust as previously assumed, and that learning biases alone might not straightforwardly explain the typological tendencies. This challenges the link between learning biases and typological distributions, suggesting that pronominal paradigms evolve in a manner that is less constrained by learning biases, and/or that alternative processing and communicative biases may better account for cross-linguistic distributions of pronominal number neutralisation.

articles.title: Cross-linguistic regularities in pronominal numberneutralisation are not driven by learning biases: Limits of theTypological Prevalence Hypothesis for morphosyntactic
articles.authors: Carmen Saldana, Chundra Cathcart, Jessica Ivani, Balthasar Bickel, Mora Maldonado
articles.abstract: Number neutralisation—the loss of singular-plural distinctions—is one of the most common homophony patterns in pronominal paradigms across languages but follows systematic asymmetries across person values. Specifically, number distinctions are claimed to be most frequently neutralised in third person, less so in second person, and least often in first person. While this generalisation has been widely noted, its empirical foundation to date remains relatively weak, and no clear mechanistic explanation has been established for why this typological asymmetry might arise. To address this gap, we test the Typological Prevalence Hypothesis (TPH)—which predicts that more frequent linguistic patterns should be easier to learn—as a potential explanation for these cross-linguistic patterns. We first conduct a large-scale synchronic analysis of pronominal paradigms (1,250 languages), confirming a frequency-based hierarchy (3rd > 2nd > 1st) but challenging its previously assumed implicational nature (i.e., if 1st, then 2nd, and if 2nd, then 3rd). A diachronic phylogenetic analysis finds weaker evidence for this frequency effect but stronger for the implicational aspect. Finally, an artificial language learning experiment testing the learnability of different neutralisation patterns reveals that learners do not mirror typological tendencies: contrary to predictions—and in line with a speaker-based bias—first-person neutralisation is easiest to acquire. These findings suggest that the typological evidence for the homophony hierarchy might not be as clear as previously assumed, and that learning biases alone might not straightforwardly explain typological regularities. This challenges the TPH, suggesting that pronominal paradigms evolve in a manner that is less constrained by learning pressures, and/or that alternative processing and communicative pressures may better account for cross-linguistic distributions of pronominal number neutralisation.

articles.title: Civic demands, hidden descent: survey mode and the measurement of naturalisation attitudes in Germany, 1996–2023
articles.abstract: The shift from descent-based to civic naturalisation criteria is a well-established finding in German integration research. However, this finding stems from a single ALLBUS battery consistently administered face-to-face. In 2023, ALLBUS implemented a randomised experiment comparing interviewer-administered and self-administered designs. We used this experiment to explore whether the observed decline reflects evolving public opinion and respondents’ willingness to express certain views to an interviewer. Our findings indicate that, in the absence of an interviewer, the proportion of respondents who consider ‘born in Germany’ important increases by 21.6 percentage points, and ‘German descent’ by 15.2 percentage points. Conversely, demands regarding migrants’ conduct show minimal change. Respondents who emphasise descent do not form a separate group with a purely ethnic view of citizenship; most also strongly advocate for civic criteria. This suggests that ascriptive demands accompany, rather than replace, civic demands. The extent to which this accounts for the decline observed between 1996 and 2023 depends on the unobserved interviewer gap in 1996. For ‘born in Germany’, this share is bounded between approximately zero and 53 per cent. While ascriptive criteria did decline, the reduction was likely less pronounced than indicated by the face-to-face record. As ALLBUS is now self-administered, continuing the series without a mode correction would erroneously suggest an ethnic resurgence.

articles.title: The waning role of sociology in adult learning? Comparative disciplinary language in course offerings at German adult education centers since the 1950s
articles.abstract: We provide evidence on the role of sociology in adult learning, and how this changed over time compared to economics and anthropology. Data from adult education centers in Germany (Volkshochschulen) from the German Institute for Adult Education’s VHS-statistics and VHS-programme-archive program brochures are used with text mining and natural language processing methods to identify discipline-specific changes in rates of courses and contents. When combined with national statistics the text-as-data generates a picture of the relevance of sociology in adult learning in Germany. The results show a long-run decline in the visibility and provision of sociology in VHS adult learning since its peak in the 1970s–1980s, with sociology losing institutional ground compared to economics and converging toward the consistently lower levels observed for anthropology.

articles.title: Large language models made social science claims more assertive
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now edit much of the scientific literature, and models tuned on human feedback avoid expressing uncertainty. We asked whether LLM editing changed how strongly social scientists state their findings. In 420,526 abstracts from 1,445 social-science journals published in 2015-2026, the estimated share of sentences matching text edited by GPT-4o-family models rose from about 2% in 2019-22 to 52% in 2026. Against the 2015-22 trend, abstracts of 2024-26 contained 14% fewer modal hedges such as may and a third more strong verbs such as demonstrate. In a coded subsample of 14,527 abstracts, the share with an unhedged causal claim rose 4.2 percentage points beyond the 2019--22 trend. Across 917 journals, the fall in hedges and the rise in evidential verbs grew with uptake and appeared only after ChatGPT; for strong verbs this link partly reflects earlier trends, but it held within first authors. Editing 200 abstracts from 2019-22 with the GPT-4o family, the most widely used in 2023-25, removed hedges, doubled strong verbs and added implied causal claims in amounts comparable to the journal-level changes, and blind readers judged edits made for a leading journal as stating findings more strongly. GPT-5 mini still removed hedges and added implied causal claims; the current GPT-6 models added no strong verbs and no net unhedged causal claims; and Claude Sonnet 5.5 did not make abstracts more assertive. LLM editing has made the social-science record state its findings more strongly, and how much depends on the model authors use.

articles.title: Protective Opacity: Xenophobic Violence, Immigrant Entrepreneurs and the Erosion of Evidence on Economic Loss
articles.abstract: When immigrant-owned shops are looted, the damage is plain to everyone on the street and seldom set down in a record that an official, a court or a relief scheme could use. This conceptual paper traces part of the reason to how owners protect themselves when the state does not. Immigrant entrepreneurs who fear collective attack, and doubt that the state will protect them, may deliberately cut their business's official or public profile, a response the paper calls protective opacity. Where many owners also cut their records and independent sources cannot fill the gap, the sector would lack the records to show what it contributes and loses (a collective evidentiary externality), and losses would become harder to recognise and attribute. The paper sets out propositions on adaptation, documentation and political response, with a research design to separate the mechanism from appropriation, impunity and motivated reasoning. South Africa is used to specify the mechanism, which has not yet been tested. Its central prediction is that, where violence and political incentives are similar, localities that hold better records before an attack will document the losses that follow more completely. It also sets out disconfirmation criteria and ways to strengthen sector-level evidence without exposing individual enterprises.

articles.title: Talking America Back from the Cliff—Messengers and Messages to Prevent Political Violence: Findings from a Nationally Representative Survey
articles.authors: Garen Wintemute, Krista Neumann, Bradley Velasquez, Sonia Robinson, Shaina Sta Cruz, Julia Schleimer, Aaron Shev, Daniel Tancredi, Elizabeth A. Tomsich, Mona A. Wright

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Background: Trusted-messenger interventions are effective in preventing or mitigating many health problems, but their application to political violence has not been examined. This study explores how frequently persons who are willing to commit political violence are open to persuasion otherwise and assesses the potential effectiveness of specific messengers and messages at inducing that change. Methods: Findings are from Wave 5 (conducted May 15-June 15, 2026) of a nationally representative annual longitudinal survey of us adults. A new sample of young adults (ages 18-21y) was added in 2026, as no existing cohort members were in that age range. Survey respondents were included in this analysis if they were “very willing” or “completely willing” to commit political violence. Outcomes of primary interest were messengers and messages that respondents considered potentially effective (and most effective) in persuading them to be unwilling to commit violence. Secondary analyses categorized respondents by sociodemographic characteristics, political party and Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement affiliations, firearm ownership and use, and approval of right- and left-wing extremist organizations and movements. Results: The survey completion rate was 88.4%. Of 8,448 respondents, 1,058 (12.5%) met the eligibility criterion. A large majority of these respondents (n = 867; 77.4%, 95% CI 73.0%, 81.2%) reported that at least 1 messenger (n = 610) or message (n = 837) might make them unwilling to commit political violence. Respondents most frequently identified family members (34.8%, 95% CI 30.8%, 39.1%) and friends (29.1%, 95% CI 25.3%, 33.2%) as effective from a list of 8 messengers. Among 6 values-oriented messages, “violence is not who you are” was most often cited as potentially effective (36.5% of respondents, 95% CI 31.5%, 39.8%). Among 8 pragmatic messages, “violence could end up with you in prison or jail” was cited most often (36.7% of respondents, 95% CI 32.6%, 41.0%); 4 others were cited at similar frequencies. There was surprisingly little variation in messenger and message selection across respondent subgroups. Conclusions: Among the small proportion of respondents reporting a high degree of willingness to commit political violence, a large majority were open to change in response to interventions by trusted messengers—and willing to provide information in support of those interventions. These findings support targeted messaging for political violence prevention and suggest that large-scale prevention efforts are feasible and may be effective.

articles.title: Do We "Simply not Know"? A history of how economists model the future
articles.authors: Beatrice Cherrier, Thomas Delcey, Aurélien Goutsmedt, Aurélien Saïdi

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Most economic models speak about the future, yet economists do not see themselves as specialists of the future and seldom state what they take it to be: determined or open, reversible or not, repeating the past or not. They have nonetheless engaged with it in two ways: by modeling how economic agents see it, chiefly through expectations, and through assumptions that reveal how modelers themselves conceive it (stationarity, dynamics, horizon, reversibility). In doing so, they refined notions such as uncertainty, risk, time, intertemporal choice and expectations, which are also the categories through which historians of economics have studied this work. In this paper, we review both literatures: how economists have modeled the future over the past century, and how historians have documented these models. We argue that the canonical models of the 1940s and 1950s "tamed" the future by implicitly treating it as determinate, timeless and fictional. Later work in finance, in policy institutions and in theory sought, respectively, to price, to govern and to reopen this future.

articles.title: Engage With Caution: Computational “Big Data” Geography, Recycled Cybernetic Buzzwords, and a Pragmatic Critique of AI and Smart Urbanism

subjects.name: Social and Philosophical Foundations of Education
Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Computational, “smart” , and “Big Data” geography has resurged amid the post-2022 generative “Artificial Intelligence” hype cycle, marketed as a fourth Kuhnian paradigm rendering social theory obsolete. Drawing on Nietzschean genealogy, this paper argues that “Artificial Intelligence” and “Smart Cities” are neither novel nor coherent breakthroughs. Like the faded “Metaverse” , “Crypto” , and “Digital Twins” , they operate as “essentially contested concepts” and rhetorical proxies for the future of technology—allowing salesmen, venture capital, and grant ecosystems to reify social relations into commoditised data while ignoring the structural impossibility of realising such buzzwords as conceived. Crucially, this triumphalism revives the unexamined rationalism of the 1950s–1960s Quantitative Revolution, whose cybernetic determinism, “McNamara fallacies” , and high-modernist schemes provoked the 1962 Lund backlash, David Harvey’s critique of “counter-revolutionary theory” , and the 1970s critical turns. Reading Weber, Haraway, and Scott against this lineage exposes how algorithmic models commit the “god trick” , foster 30,000-foot apophenia, and legitimise a posteriori surveillance, predictive policing, and dispossession through “thin simplifications” erasing local mêtis. Refusing a Manichean rejection of computation, the paper mobilises pragmatism and Taylor Shelton’s strategic positivism, evaluating algorithms by present utility over the longue durée and providing ways in which to ground their utility within pragmatic research paradigms.

articles.title: Verified Lexical Correspondences between Ishakkoy (Atakapa) and Louisiana French Creole: An Audit of the Evidence in Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletins 108 and 43 and Kaufman's Atakapa Ishakkoy Dictionary
articles.abstract: This paper audits the evidence for lexical contact between Ishakkoy (Atakapa), a language isolate of the Gulf Coast, and Louisiana French Creole, Louisiana's French-lexified Creole. Ishakkoy has no known relatives, so no word the two languages share can have come down from a common ancestor. Whatever they hold in common was passed from neighbor to neighbor, in the bilingual enclaves of Southwest Louisiana, where Ishakkoy-speaking and Creole-speaking households lived side by side. Every candidate is tested against the primary documentary record — Gatschet and Swanton's Dictionary of the Atakapa Language (Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 108, 1932) and Swanton's Bulletin 43 (1911) — against a verified Louisiana French Creole lexicon (Ti Liv Kréyòl, 2nd ed., 2020), and against David V. Kaufman's Atakapa Ishakkoy Dictionary (2nd ed., 2022). Six correspondences hold up on the documentary record. Four passed from Ishakkoy into Louisiana French Creole and the regional vernacular: plaquemine 'persimmon' and the place-names Calcasieu, Mermentau, and Opelousas. Two are French/Creole loans into Ishakkoy: kapi' 'coffee' and A'léman 'German'. Three more French loans into Ishakkoy appear in Kaufman's dictionary alone; they are reported separately, in a scholarly tier of their own. Eight well-known candidates — bayou, chaoui, and tasso among them — are rejected: they reached Creole from Choctaw or Spanish, with no Ishakkoy leg. The word for 'pecan' turns out to be a parallel borrowing, drawn from a third source through French. And a similarity pass over the everyday core vocabulary finds no resemblance at all in nine of nine core concepts. The deepest evidence of contact is not lexical but documentary: Bulletin 108 preserves nine French glosses inside its own entries, along with two contemporary attestations of the bilingual enclave. Every count in this audit is a floor, not a ceiling.

articles.title: The Structural Disadvantage of Active and Leveraged Retail Trading: Cross-National Evidence, Multi-Horizon Survival, and Proprietary-Trading Contract Economics
articles.abstract: Short-term, leveraged retail trading has expanded rapidly, but one-year nominal returns and isolated trade outcomes understate the cumulative cost of active speculation. We review regulatory and peer-reviewed evidence across fourteen market settings (data years 1991–2024) and pool five independent loss-rate estimates from regulator- or exchange-based records (about 11.6 million individuals and accounts, 98% from India's SEBI census) in a random-effects meta-analysis, complemented by parametric absorbing-barrier survival modeling and institutional analysis. Logit-scale REML-HKSJ pooling yields an 88.70% net-loser rate (95% CI: 68.09%–96.65%; 85.3%–88.7% across specifications), with higher losses in multi-year derivatives cohorts (93.81%) than in annual CFD cohorts (74.46%), though horizon overlaps with instrument and jurisdiction. A companion Bayesian stress test yields a 99.74% posterior probability of majority loss (≥94.1% under severe bias, dependence, or 50% noise contamination), alongside a 74.0% median 12-month loss rate across 53 regulated UK and EU CFD brokers. Parametric log-wealth diffusion with a 90% ruin barrier implies breakeven median gross-alpha hurdles of 19.1% to 110.6% per year: even a +10%/yr gross edge leaves 10-year economic loss probabilities of 88.65% to >99.99%, while domestic inflation cuts three-year local-currency 10x survival to 3.01% in Turkey and 0.15% in Iran. Finally, 25,000-path intraday simulations of 2026 proprietary-trading contracts document 0.38%–4.48% retail first-payout survival and negative retail expected monetary value across all regimes, persisting for skilled traders (Sharpe +0.50) under strict trailing drawdowns with consistency caps (except marginal +$10.85 on Topstep 50K). Even over short one- to three-year horizons, empirical censuses show that surviving winners rarely earn above modest wage-level income (0.5% above $54/day in Brazil; ~1% above ~$1,200 over three years in India), and over 15–20 years, modeled economic survival approaches zero.

articles.title: The Geography of Pet Insurance in the United States: State Distribution of Insured Pets and Premium Dollars, 2025
articles.abstract: This paper assembles and analyses the state-level distribution of the United States pet insurance market published by the North American Pet Health Insurance Association (NAPHIA) in its 2026 State of the Industry Report (calendar-year 2025 data). At year-end 2025, 5.23 million dogs and 1.75 million cats were insured in the United States, yet penetration remained low: 5.99% of dogs and 2.29% of cats. Total gross written premium reached $5.7 billion, and the average accident-and-illness premium was $836 per year for a dog and $435 for a cat. The market is geographically concentrated: California alone held 18.1% of insured pets and 19.9% of premium, and the four largest states held 37.8% of insured pets and 40.1% of premium. Because NAPHIA publishes state shares but not state average premiums, we compute a premium intensity index - a state's share of premium divided by its share of insured pets - as a transparent measure of relative premium levels. The index is highest in Massachusetts and Connecticut (1.18) and lowest, among states with a measurable base, in Oklahoma (0.60). We document the index's construction, its species- and plan-mix limitations, and why it should not be read as a state price. Situating the market in the social-science literature on household financial protection, insurance demand, and geographic inequality in access to veterinary care, we argue that the state distribution is best read as a map of where households have converted the financial risk of veterinary care into a fixed premium — and, by implication, where most have not.

articles.title: Gender, Genes, and Income: How Equality of Opportunity Changed in Norway Across the 20th Century
articles.authors: Martin Isungset, Tina Baier, Torkild Hovde Lyngstad
articles.abstract: The gender income gap shrank dramatically in Western democracies over the twentieth century. We ask how genetic influences (heritability) and gendered shared environments in lifetime income changed across birth cohorts. We interpret heritability as achievement and gendered shared environments as social ascription by gender. Our data are from 11,668 twin pairs born in Norway between 1915 and 1994, linked with full-population administrative income data covering 1967–2023. The heritability of lifetime income more than tripled across birth cohorts, from 17 to 56 percent. The rise in heritability and the decline in gendered shared environments suggest growing equality of opportunity between genders over time. Yet, equality of opportunity was low until very recently, even in Norway, an extensive welfare state where gender equality has been a political priority since the 1950s. We also ask whether heritability differs between women and men, when women and men are analyzed separately. Here, heritability is lower for women, suggesting that genetic endowments are converted into income less fully for women than for men. We argue that genetically informed designs can evaluate equality of opportunity between genders, though many interpretive challenges remain.

articles.title: Compounding Disadvantage: Childhood Health and Black-White Economic Inequality over the Life Course
articles.abstract: Childhood health has consistently been shown to predict later labor market and human capital outcomes, and many of the structural barriers that drive racial economic disparities also produce disparities in child health. Using data from the Health and Retirement Study linked to Social Security Administration earnings records, I ask whether childhood health compounds racial economic inequality across the life course. I find that poorer childhood health is associated with disproportionately large reductions in earnings and employment for Black respondents compared to White respondents. In Oaxaca-Blinder decompositions, up to 2.4% of the earnings gap and 12.2% of the employment gap can be attributed to childhood health, with contributions increasing with age in a manner consistent with cumulative disadvantage. Conversely, childhood health has little role in shaping Black wealth accumulation or Black-White wealth gaps, suggesting childhood health is a domain-specific mechanism of cumulative racial disadvantage. (Stone Center on Socio-Economic Inequality Working Paper)

articles.title: A Decade of Change in Adolescents’ Life Satisfaction Across PISA Countries: Recent Recovery and a Mixed Picture
articles.authors: Jose Marquez, Wanying Zhou, Leoni Boyle, Laura Taylor
articles.abstract: Adolescent wellbeing declines in the 2010s and early 2020s have been documented in many countries. This includes widespread life satisfaction declines among 15-year-olds in PISA-participating countries in 2015–2022, especially among girls. We study whether that pattern continued in 2025 and how the decade-long trend varied across countries. We estimated changes within countries in mean life satisfaction (0–10) and in the percentage of students reporting low life satisfaction (4 or less), and compared fixed sets of countries, giving each country equal weight in international averages. We also examined differences by gender, socioeconomic status, and immigrant background. Between 2022 and 2025, mean life satisfaction increased significantly (p<.05) in 60 of 65 countries, and decreased significantly in one. The average percentage of students reporting low life satisfaction fell from 16.5% to 12.6%. Girls’ mean rose by 0.68 points and boys’ by 0.22 points. Girls’ gains exceeded boys’ significantly in 57 countries. The average boy–girl gap narrowed from 0.77 to 0.31 points. Across 40 countries observed in all four cycles, the average fell from 7.42 in 2015 to 7.14 in 2018 and 6.85 in 2022, then rose to 7.30 in 2025, while the percentage reporting low life satisfaction remained 2.0 percentage points above its 2015 level. Changes in socioeconomic and immigrant background gaps were smaller and less consistent across countries. The 2025 results show widespread improvements in life satisfaction, particularly among girls, following earlier declines. However, both mean life satisfaction and the prevalence of low life satisfaction remained worse than in 2015, with substantial variation across countries.

articles.title: The Power of Longitudinal Study Designs and Their Applications in Global Academic Career Research
articles.abstract: This paper outlines longitudinal theoretical and methodological frameworks for studying global academic careers. Longitudinal studies focus on whole career trajectories as the primary units of analysis; thus, time becomes a key component in explaining what happens to academic careers. Using the sociology of life course and path dependency as a point of departure, this research examines how scientists move from one position to another and how they stay in certain positions or leave them (productivity, impact, and elite status). The proposed framework of longitudinal study designs combines existing methodologies to address a single issue: the temporal structure of academic careers. Sequence analysis (which identifies sequences of events) is combined with survival models (which measure how long an individual remains in a particular position), and transition models (which model changes between positions). Additionally, the author distinguishes between three forms of time—calendar, cohort, and career—highlighting the impact of different observational time horizons.
