The longitudinal agenda includes notions such as career closure, turning points, conversions between productivity, journal prestige, and citation impact, as well as hidden global career types, collaboration shocks, and gender-based temporal inequality.

articles.title: Employer referral networks
articles.abstract: Employers are confronted with an information asymmetry when hiring, and rely on references from other employers to verify candidates. Such cooperation is hard to achieve, since employers are also competitors. This article examines how employers cooperate in referral networks, and which network positions benefit employers. The article leverages eight unique datasets across two Swiss sectors — childcare and fiduciary services. Using exponential random graph models (ERGMs), it first analyses how organizational attributes and network dynamics shape cooperation. Second, using auto-logistic actor attribute models (ALAAMs), it analyses which network positions help employers overcome hiring difficulties. Third, it analyses which organizations occupy the network’s center. The results show that the two sectors differ regarding the existence of an established prestige hierarchy. Fiduciary firms are ranked by prestige, with the most prestigious at the network center, whereas the childcare sector does not exhibit such a prestige order. Prestige being a public signal of a firm’s reliability allows fiduciary firms to rely less on observing local network structures to ensure cooperation. Local network structures still play a role, however. Fiduciaries still select alters already trusted by one of their connections (close open triads hierarchically). Childcare has no comparable prestige hierarchy. Absent a ranking to organize around, they select trustworthy alters rolling over expectations from their existing connections to a new counterpart (hierarchic triadic closure). In addition, they select alters that depend on someone who in turn depends on them, so they are in a position to sanction them (horizontal triadic closure). The two sectors also reward different network positions: with a prestige hierarchy ensuring cooperation, fiduciary firms benefit from referrals reaching their one's own circle, while childcare organizations benefit when they close a triad. The article makes two contributions. Empirically, it offers the first systematic analysis of employer referral networks. Theoretically, it translates the two main rationales for triadic closure proposed by the literature — rolling-over of expectations, and sanctioning — to directed networks. It offers a rationale for each form of closure in directed networks: hierarchical closure enables selection, whereas cyclic closure enables sanctioning. Whereas selection is relevant independent of context, sanctioning gains relevance in absence of a prestige hierarchy.

articles.title: Governmental regulation of youth social media access worldwide: A living database and interactive dashboard
articles.authors: Qiyang Zhang, Yueyin Ni, Nithin Weerasinghe, Yile Yang, Zhuo Ma, Cameron Tan, Zhiying Yue
articles.abstract: Governments worldwide are rapidly adopting policies that restrict young people’s access to social media, yet no global, verified record of these policies exists. We present a living database and interactive dashboard (https://social-media-policy-map.vercel.app/) documenting 155 government policies across 106 countries. Each record was coded independently by one researcher and verified by another using a standard coding framework, with announcement, enactment, and effective dates recorded separately. Policy announcements rose from 17 in January 2023 to 128 in October 2026, but only 50 had entered into force. Among national-level policy records, this gap largely reflects recency: 80% of policies announced between 2023 and 2024 were in force as of October 2026. In US states, by contrast, over half of policies had failed, been struck down, or been suspended. Policies varied widely, with age thresholds ranging from 13 to 18 and mechanisms ranging from outright bans to parental consent, with child safety as the most commonly stated rationale. The resource supports policy evaluation, cross-jurisdiction comparison, and public understanding.

articles.title: Shrinking women: Why successfully engaging in strength training is harder for women – a bone perspective.
articles.authors: Riccarda Albana Quattlaender, Tania Crotti, Mark R Hutchinson, Tim Lathlean, A/Prof Paul Rothmore
articles.abstract: Women face an increased risk of osteoporosis characterized by low bone mineral density (BMD). Heavy strength training (ST) is recommended to enhance BMD which is crucial for successful prevention of osteoporosis. However, with women underrepresented in gyms, a minimal proportion engage in ST as recommended for enhancing BMD. Consequently, this study aimed to identify barriers impacting women’s access to and success in ST aimed at enhancing BMD. Eight focus groups were conducted, involving 28 healthy women over 45 years of age. Participants were part of the ST intervention groups of a pilot RCT designed for osteoporosis prevention. Pre-intervention, participants did not engage in regular ST for at least 12 months. During the intervention, they engaged in supervised ST sessions twice weekly over six months in small groups. On completion, participants were interviewed within training groups. Reflexive thematic analysis was performed, employing a critical realist onto-epistemology. Four themes were developed: T1: My time isn’t mine; T2: Medical neglect & gaslighting weaken me throughout life; T3: My body: a disappointing thing, not a strong performer; T4: Gym: a man’s world, I don’t belong. We interpret these barriers as shaped by structural discrimination inhibiting access to ST and undermining training success, which may render ST ineffective for bone health. Moreover, T1-3 may erode women’s health, reducing exercise capacity. We propose that society contributes to conditions that ‘shrink’ women mentally and physically, which may increase the risk of frailty, fracture and disability.

articles.title: Homicidal violence and childhood bereavement in Mexico: Parental loss and kinship inequalities 2000–2024
articles.authors: Mary Carolina Sosa Bonilla, Víctor Manuel García-Guerrero, Diego Alburez-Gutierrez
articles.abstract: The increase in homicides in Mexico has disrupted the gains in survival over the last two decades. Prior demographic research has focused on its impact on mortality and forced migration. However, its consequences for surviving children remain understudied. To fill this research gap, we estimate annual maternal, paternal, and any parental loss in Mexico during 2000–2024 and examine regional inequalities to account for geographic variations in the evolution of criminal violence and insecurity. We combine vital death registration data from INEGI with demographic reconciliation and population projections from CONAPO. We implemented time-varying, two-sex kinship models in DemoKin using sex-specific survival and a common fertility schedule for both sexes. Causespecific deaths and expected parental age distributions yield approximate annual loss probabilities and population counts. Our main cause of death combines homicides and events of undetermined intent. Paternal loss increased sharply after 2007, with another increase after 2015. In 2020, the estimated losses reached 59,569 for fathers and 65,322 for at least one parent. Regional peaks differed in timing, with the Northwest, Pacific, and North-Central regions having particularly high paternal loss probabilities. Other external causes remained the largest source of maternal loss nationally. Unequal mortality conditions are reflected in unequal exposure to parental bereavement during childhood. Annual loss estimates do not measure orphanhood prevalence, grief, or causal effects of anti-drug policies. Ours is the first analysis linking cause-specific mortality to formal kinship demography that quantifies the scale and territorial distribution of parental loss while distinguishing individual probabilities from population burden.

articles.title: Private demand cannot scale carbon sequestration
articles.authors: Matthew G. Burgess, Hassan Elshayeb, Sanju Patel, Elizabeth Francis, Finbar Curtin, Ian Burgess

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Scenarios meeting international climate change targets assume tens of gigatons of annual anthropogenic carbon sequestration by mid-to-late century. Ecosystems of voluntary carbon markets, corporate climate pledges, and sustainable banking initiatives assume private capital is key to delivering this. Yet voluntary carbon markets currently provide only tens of megatons of sequestration, and vintages are declining. We argue that private incentives can contribute at most marginally to multi-gigaton- scale sequestration demand. Carbon sequestration is a public good. Marketing incentives driving carbon credit demand are small and disconnected from scaling, expected storage, and costs. Scaling demand through public pressure would be unprecedented, and public pressure seems to be declining. Scaling demand through financial firms faces antitrust and fiduciary duty challenges, illustrated by the Net-Zero Banking Alliance’s collapse. Sequestration projects’ monetizable co-benefits, when existing, may not scale with sequestration. Governments should accelerate interventions to facilitate carbon sequestration, de-emphasize high-sequestration scenarios in climate outlooks, or both.

articles.title: Putting Claims on the Map: Environmental Registration and Deforestation
articles.abstract: On the Amazon frontier, clearing forest is a way to claim land. We ask whether deforestation falls when landholders can instead register a claim. Brazil's Rural Environmental Registry (CAR) records self-declared boundaries without adjudicating property rights. We estimate changes in deforestation following first observed registration using staggered difference-in-differences models, 353,748 CAR records, and annual land-use data from 2001 to 2024. We estimate a decline in annual deforestation after registration of 20% of the treated pre-registration mean. Some declarations overlap other CAR claims, protected areas, or undesignated public forests, indicating competing claims or intersections with public land. The estimated decline varies across territorial contexts. It is 13% where the declared boundary overlaps no other registered claim, protected area, or undesignated public forest, and 56% where it overlaps undesignated public forest. These patterns are consistent with registration substituting for clearing as a signal of possession and registrants anticipating greater administrative scrutiny.

articles.title: Technogendering of the Digital Economy (TDE): From Fragmented Gender Approaches to an Integrated Feminist Framework
articles.abstract: Digital technologies were promised as a lever for gender equality. Yet the digital economy is not gender-neutral: it is designed within existing gender relations, it redraws the boundary between paid and unpaid work, and it draws value from feminised work that is rarely counted. Research on these processes remains fragmented. A systematic review published in 2021 found gender analysis of the digital economy spread across three approaches, feminist theories of technology, feminist political economy and mainstream economics, without shared theoretical ground. This article answers its call for a more integrated approach. It reads that fragmentation as a disciplinary division of labour, in which each approach isolates one moment of a single process, from the design of a system to the global organisation of value. Rereading through this typology the corpus of a feminist scoping review (2010–2025), it suggests that the division persists among feminist research. The article then presents the Technogendering of the Digital Economy (TDE) framework, a feminist analytical framework for studying how gender, technology and work are co-produced. The framework is operationalised through four analytical dimensions, each tied to a moment in the life of a digital system: the technological mediation of gender, algorithmic abstraction and bias, gendered regimes of algorithmic governance, and global inequalities of digital labour and data extraction. FemTech illustrates how these dimensions may reinforce one another, from the design of cycle-tracking apps to the global circulation of reproductive data and value. Followed to the global scale, the analysis leads to a proposal: the feminist study of the digital economy should be understood as a field of feminist international political economy.

articles.title: The association between gambling behaviour and sleep problems: an umbrella review
articles.authors: Su Golder, Alexandra Nazarova, Greg Forshaw, Amanda E Perry, Scott Cairney
articles.abstract: Introduction: Understanding the relationship between gambling behaviour and sleep is important for developing interventions to reduce harm. Whilst gambling problems may disrupt sleep, insufficient sleep may also increase gambling through impaired judgement or providing an activity during sleeping hours. This umbrella review synthesised evidence on the association between gambling and sleep, including the direction of this relationship. Methods: We searched KSR Evidence database, Google Scholar, key websites, conducted forward and backward citation searching, and contacted authors and experts. We included systematic reviews published since 2015 examining associations between gambling and sleep problems in any direction and population. Results: From 391 articles screened, eleven systematic reviews were included containing 34 primary studies (30 unique) with minimal overlap (Corrected Covered Area 1.33%). Eight reviews examined gambling as the exposure and sleep as the outcome, one examined sleep as the exposure, one examined both directions, and in one the direction was unclear. Consistent associations were found between gambling and sleep problems, including sleep loss, insomnia, poor sleep quality, sleep deprivation and use of sleep medication. Sleep harms also extended to concerned significant others. Evidence was predominantly cross-sectional, and validated sleep measures were rarely used. Nine of the 11 reviews were rated as low or critically low quality using AMSTAR 2. Conclusion: We found consistent associations between gambling and sleep problems in people who gamble and in their concerned significant others. However, the direction and causality of the relationship remains uncertain. Further research is needed to understand the potentially complex relationship between sleep and gambling.

articles.title: Democratic Support Is Conditional on Social Norms: How Citizens' Perceptions of a Democratic Consensus Matter
articles.authors: Daniel Bischof, Tim Lars Allinger, Morgan Le Corre Juratic, Kristian Frederiksen
articles.abstract: Democratic stability is often said to rest on a social consensus over democratic values. Yet this consensus is usually inferred from aggregating individual attitudes rather than measured in its social nature -- as citizens' perceptions of what others support. We conceptualize democratic consensus as a perceived social environment (social norm) and argue that democratic support is conditional on it: citizens should be more willing to support and defend democracy when they believe democratic commitments are widely shared. We study this perceived consensus by mapping it across 14 democracies and assessing its consequences with embedded vignette experiments and quasi-experimental interview-mode evidence. Citizens generally perceive broad support for democracy, but this consensus is uneven and socially fragmented. Perceiving no consensus reduces democratic support, increases acceptance of attacks on political institutions, and weakens willingness to defend democratic commitments publicly. Democratic resilience may therefore be fragile even where democratic attitudes appear stable.

articles.title: Norm Spillover: Evidence from BLM Protests
articles.abstract: Norms regulate many human interactions, but how do individuals learn about them? We theorize that such learning often happens in bundles. Norms exhibit a hierarchical structure, with lower-level, specific norms nested into higher-level, abstract ones. Strong signals about a lower-level norm can make individuals update about the higher-level norm, moving their priors about other norms that are also nested inside it. We argue that protests are one way by which this process takes place. Studying the Black Lives Matter movement following the killing of George Floyd, we show that they made Americans more favorable toward other historically marginalized groups—including those not defined by race or ethnicity (gay and lesbian individuals). Consistent with norm change, the strength of these effects depends on the partisanship of the area where respondents live more than on their own partisanship. These results show that protests can have wide-reaching effects and help understand how individuals learn about different norms.

articles.title: Bounded Responsiveness: Housing Markets and the Subnational Diversification of Programmatic Supply
articles.authors: Denis Cohen, Tim Lars Allinger, Andreas Kuepfer
articles.abstract: Political research documents important demand-side effects of geographical housing inequality. However, less is known about political supply: parties’ programmatic responses to uneven housing pressures. We propose a theory of bounded responsiveness that explains how district candidates diversify party appeals in territorial representation systems. Local housing pressures incentivize candidates to politicize housing, but party ownership and national party brands constrain how they do so: rather than openly deviating from the party line, candidates selectively emphasize party-owned policy instruments while critically engaging with competitors’ policies. Using more than two million social media posts from German MPs, combining LLM-based issue and position classification with Bayesian hierarchical shrinkage estimators, we find empirical support for our theory: cross-sectional and longitudinal evidence shows that MPs in high-cost housing markets emphasize housing more strongly, primarily through party-consistent appeals. These findings reveal how subnational economic heterogeneity shapes parties’ programmatic supply while preserving partisan constraint.

articles.title: Length of residence and belonging to place: Quick formation and the selection of stayers
articles.abstract: Urban research has long held that belonging to a neighbourhood grows with time. Most evidence for this compares different people at one point in time, and so cannot separate the effect of time from who stays. I follow almost 70,000 people across five waves of the UK Household Longitudinal Study (2009–22), observing belonging before and after more than 16,000 moves, and link one wave to more than 6,500 census neighbourhoods. Comparing different people, belonging rises steadily with length of residence: those who have lived at their address for 30 years or more are 16 percentage points more likely to belong than those who arrived in the past year, and the gap remains when differences between neighbourhoods are taken into account. Following the same people, belonging rises by about five points in the first two years at an address and much more slowly after that, which suggests that much of that gap reflects who stays rather than how long they have stayed. Belonging falls before people move, and within about three years, movers belong as much as comparable residents who stayed. Because belonging is acquired quickly after a move, part of what threatens it in places with high turnover may be that residents keep moving.

articles.title: Managed interdependence as tactic in pursuit of European digital sovereignty: the case of knowledge networks
articles.abstract: Europe’s pursuit of digital sovereignty mainly relies on two responses, regu-lating foreign technology and building domestic alternatives. But regulation has done little to grow Europe’s own digital industry, while its reach beyond the single market depends on international and corporate cooperation the Union cannot enforce. Industrial policy struggles to consistently pick winners and often only shifts dependence to another layer of the stack. We develop a third option, managed interdependence, through which a middle power shapes mutual interdependence by developing and providing access to select elements of the digital stack others depend on. While this does not offset de-pendence on others, it provides some leverage to manage this interdepend-ence by establishing and highlighting its mutual characteristics. This distinguishes it from weaponised interdependence. It recognises asymmetric power and dependence but tries to leverage institutional arrangements that are announced in advance, reciprocal, and reversible. We illustrate this through knowledge networks, where Europe’s position is strongest in the digital stack and least recognised. We close with three policy options, recog-nising, cultivating and conditioning managed interdependence through knowledge hubs.

articles.title: Fewer Branches, No Wider Gender Gap: Bank Branch Closures and Women’s Account Ownership and Use in the European Union, 2011–2024
articles.authors: Massimo Arnone, Angelo Leogrande, Alberto Costantiello, Carlo Drago, Ada Spiru
articles.abstract: Between 2011 and 2024 the number of bank branches per 100,000 adults in the European Union fell by about half. A common concern is that this shift to digital channels excludes groups that rely more on branches, including women. This paper tests that concern with five Global Findex waves for the 27 Member States, measuring the gender gap directly as the male-minus-female difference in account and debit-card ownership. The main finding is a null result: the fall in branch density was not accompanied by a wider gender gap. In fixed-effects estimates, the observed fall implies a change in the account gap of −0.25 percentage points (95% CI −1.78 to 1.27); weighting by sampling variance narrows the interval to −1.25 to 0.67, and equivalence tests reject a widening of one point or more. The result holds in long differences, in stacked fractional models and in wider OECD and European samples. A positive association between branch density and the debit-card gap disappears in log-odds and after correction for multiple testing. By contrast, the gender gap in women’s own digital access is strongly associated with the financial gap (r = 0.70 in 2024). Clustering identifies three regimes, including five Central and Eastern European countries where the gap turned against women, which closed the fewest branches. Machine-learning models cannot predict the gap within the EU. The results are descriptive associations, not causal effects.

articles.title: Is Authentic Dating Possible?
articles.abstract: In the age of AI, authenticity in dating has become a growing concern. This short essay deconstructs the notion of authenticity in dating, arguing that while it is difficult to achieve, individuals can nevertheless strive to do so by displaying to potential partners aspects of the self that are vulnerable and "unpolished."

articles.title: Willing but unable? The fiscal context of childcare expansion in Austrian municipalities
articles.abstract: In Austria, there is broad agreement that public childcare must be expanded, and equally broad agreement that municipalities lack the funds to do so. This contribution tests this "willing but unable" narrative. Based on panel data for all 2,092 Austrian municipalities for the years 2011 to 2024, I distinguish between fiscal stress, measured by debt per capita and the municipal fiscal health score, and fiscal capacity, measured by tax revenue per capita. I combine fixed effects panel regressions with cross-sectional models within federal states. The results show that fiscal stress does not slow down childcare expansion. Fiscal capacity, in contrast, matters: municipalities with higher tax revenues expanded faster. The partisan composition of the municipal council (political supply) shows no effect, whereas the political orientation of the electorate (political demand), measured by left vote shares in national elections, is associated with higher coverage rates. Unlike in Germany, partisan effects do not depend on fiscal capacity. The findings suggest that earmarked co-funding protects childcare expansion from fiscal stress but does not compensate for differences in fiscal capacity.

articles.title: Why Protest Persists: Social Capital, Local Networks, and Collective Action in Dezful, Iran
articles.abstract: Iran has seen repeated waves of nationwide protest since 2017, reaching provincial cities well beyond the main metropolitan centres. Dezful, in Khuzestan, is one of them, and contentious mobilisation has returned there wave after wave. I ask why protest has come back so often, and what local relational structures make that recurrence possible. I pursue the question by comparing four neighbourhoods within the city: two with concentrated Bakhtiari populations and two long- established Dezfuli ones. My evidence is twenty-five semi-structured interviews, field observation during the January 2026 protests, interviews with local experts, and Persian-language sources. Recurrence, I argue, depends less on the depth of grievance, which is widely shared, than on local relational infrastructure. For this I develop the concept of mobilisable ethnicity: a configuration in which a publicly legible ethnic category coincides with dense, kinship-anchored networks concentrated enough to overlap with everyday life. Where formal political organisation is weak, this may lower the cost of coordinating and allow mobilisation to be reproduced rather than rebuilt. Respondents in the Bakhtiari neighbourhoods described participation as moving through kin and neighbourhood channels; elsewhere they described it as individual or friendship-based. I state the scope conditions, and say where the argument outruns its evidence.

articles.title: Local Politics of Water Scarcity: Territorial Fragmentation and Water Allocation in Iran’s Karkheh Basin
articles.abstract: In July 2021, severe water shortages in Iran’s Karkheh River Basin triggered widespread protests and emergency reallocation, yet restrictions were distributed unevenly across the basin. Drawing on official water-sector and parliamentary records and Persian-language sources, this article examines how local politics shapes the distribution of scarcity. It argues that hydrologically integrated resources are governed through territorially fragmented political and administrative arenas. Hydraulic position, jurisdiction and political access consequently shape whose claims receive attention and where restrictions fall. The Karkheh case reveals a broader challenge: governing interconnected resources through political institutions organised at competing territorial scales.

articles.title: When Does Negotiation Backfire? Gender, Job Levels, and Wage Demand Levels
articles.abstract: This study examines whether wage negotiation reduces hiring likelihood relative to non-negotiation, at what demand levels this penalty emerges, and how these patterns vary by the job level applied for and applicants’ gender. We argue that the legitimacy of wage demands is judged against wage standards within organizations. We conducted a factorial survey experiment with 967 individuals responsible for hiring at Japanese firms. Applicants’ gender, applied job level, and their demand levels relative to the wage standard for that level in respondents’ own organizations were varied. We then compared hiring likelihood in each condition with the non-negotiation condition using mixed-effects models. As the demand level increased, negotiation became a penalty, which emerged at lower relative demand levels for managerial than for non-managerial positions and, within each job level, at lower demand levels for women than for men. The effects of wage negotiation on hiring likelihood depend not simply on whether applicants negotiate, but on how much they demand relative to the organizational wage standard. Moreover, how much one can request without disadvantage relative to non-negotiation depends on who makes the request—a dimension of inequality distinct from inequalities in the opportunity to negotiate and in the returns to negotiation.

articles.title: Conversation Strategies for Supporting Curiosity in Heritage: Design Insights from Tour Guide Practices
articles.abstract: Conversational agents are increasingly used in heritage, but we lack design guidance on how to make their situated conversations interesting, not just accurate. Human tour guides offer an insightful and ecologically valid model of how to evoke and sustain visitor curiosity in conversation. Using video recording, participant observation, and video-stimulated recall interviews, we studied how three professional tour guides afforded visitor curiosity across seven tours and 20 visitors. Following grounded theory, we identified a repertoire of 30 conversational techniques tour guides used to prepare for, enable, trigger, sustain, and monitor visitor curiosity, and identified four design considerations for conversational heritage agents, such as framing participation norms and modelling and monitoring visitor knowledge. This expands prior HCI knowledge on designing for curiosity from interactive objects to conversations, and establishes a foundation for future translation into conversational agents.

articles.title: The Erosion of Institutional Memory and the Crisis of Governance in Somalia and Puntland: Participant Testimony and a Critical Review of the Scholarly Evidence
articles.abstract: This article makes three original claims about the relationship between administrative memory and state capacity, and tests them on the Somali case. The first, and the one on which the others depend, inverts an assumption common in state-capacity scholarship. That literature ordinarily treats administrative memory as a by-product of capable institutions: build the institution and memory follows. This article argues the direction runs the other way. Where institutional containers are absent, administrative memory persists in non-state and customary forms that substitute for formal administration without sustaining the state, so that memory stands prior to capacity rather than downstream of it. The second claim is conceptual and follows from the first: institutional and collective memory stand in a substitutive as well as a sequential relationship, so that one can carry the regulatory load of the other — which is why xeer can adjudicate disputes and al-Shabaab can run taxation and justice in the absence of any state archive. The third is analytical: suppression of administrative competence in Puntland has operated through dispersal rather than exclusion, a mechanism that leaves no excluded person to count and no rejected application to record, and is therefore invisible to the Institutional Memory in Somalia and Puntland (APA 7th) | 2 appointment-based and survey-based instruments currently used to measure administrative exclusion. Each claim is stated in falsifiable form and tested against two evidentiary foundations: first-hand participant testimony from the founding of the Puntland administration in 1998 and the reconciliation processes of the 1990s and 2000s, and a critical review of the scholarly and documentary literature set against it. The documentary record confirms the political economy of suppressed expertise and the displacement of Somali history from school curricula, and it qualifies the third claim in a productive way: the existing study of Somali police development shows that police systems re-form without documentation, which is what the substitutive account predicts. The article concludes with policy implications that follow specifically from the three claims, a research agenda addressed to their testability, and a reflection on the evidentiary status of insider testimony.

articles.title: Does the Real Exchange Rate Move the Trade Balance of a Gold Exporter? Monthly Evidence from Uzbekistan after the 2017 Exchange-Rate Unification
articles.abstract: In September 2017 Uzbekistan unified its exchange rate and devalued the soum by about half. I use the years since then to test whether the real exchange rate moves the trade balance of a commodity exporter. Gold, sold abroad by the central bank, makes up 21 to 38 percent of annual exports and follows the gold price and reserve management rather than relative prices. I therefore build a monthly series of trade in goods and services net of gold for October 2017 to August 2026, constructing the missing 2017-2020 gold months from official cumulative totals and central bank reserve data. ARDL bounds tests with finite-sample critical values show that the non-gold export-import ratio returns quickly to a stable level, but an additional test shows that the levels of the real effective exchange rate, domestic and partner activity and the gold price explain little of that level. The long-run real exchange rate elasticity is -0.54: it has the Marshall-Lerner sign but is not significant, and its 95 percent confidence interval excludes effects stronger than about -1.6. There is no J-curve and only weak evidence of asymmetry. Nineteen alternative specifications give the same picture. For Uzbekistan, the exchange rate is a weak tool for the external balance.

articles.title: When Strikes Meet Stocks: Organized Labor and the Politics of Employee Ownership
articles.abstract: This paper examines how changes in organized labor’s strength shape the adoption of employee stock ownership plans (ESOPs) in the United States. While ESOPs are often framed as cooperative institutions that improve worker welfare and firm performance, they may also function as strategic responses to union pressure on the side of management. Using Form 5500 filings from 2000 to 2024, this study exploits the staggered adoption of right-to-work laws as a shock to union strength. Difference-in-differences and event-study results show that right-to-work laws reduce union density and are followed by a decline in active ESOPs. The effect attenuates and becomes insignificant once union density is accounted for, suggesting that organized labor is a key channel linking right-to-work laws to employee ownership formation. These findings show that employee ownership is not only a firm-level compensation tool, but also part of a broader political economy of labor-management conflict.

articles.title: Rural Clustering in Ukraine: A Window of Opportunity for Sustainable Post-War Recovery and EU Integration
articles.authors: Olena Borodina, Ihor Prokopa, Viktor Yarovyi, Anna Ostapenko
articles.abstract: This analytical paper substantiates the economic and institutional rationale for reorienting Ukraine’s wartime and post-war recovery strategy toward supporting clustered smallholder agricultural producers through rural clustering as a primary driver of European integration, domestic food market supply, rural employment, and national food security. Drawing on international policy frameworks (FAO, IFAD, and the EU Common Agricultural Policy), empirical field surveys of 32 territorial food markets across Kyiv, Zhytomyr, and Kyiv Oblast (2025), and studies of internally displaced persons (IDPs) in rural areas, the authors demonstrate that smallholder farmers generate higher value added per hectare and retain capital within local communities, yet suffer from critically low institutional self-organization. Comparative analysis of post-war agricultural reconstruction in the Western Balkans—specifically IFAD-supported rural clustering models in Bosnia and Herzegovina (RCDP, READP) and Montenegro (RCTP)—confirms that horizontal and vertical clustering overcomes land fragmentation, facilitates EU food safety and quality certification, unlocks pre-accession funding (IPARD), and accelerates alignment with Chapter 11 of the EU acquis. Classifying emerging wartime cluster initiatives in Ukraine into agri-rural clusters (ARCs), agri-rural processing clusters (ARPCs), and corporate agro-industrial structures, the policy brief outlines core principles for shifting state support from direct per-hectare subsidies toward shared cluster infrastructure, professional facilitation, and rural proofing. Finally, the authors propose concrete legislative and institutional next steps ahead of opening EU Negotiating Cluster 5 in 2027, including adopting a dedicated Law of Ukraine “On Farm Clusters and Network Cooperation in the Agricultural Sector” and establishing a National Office for Rural and Farm Clustering (NORFC).

articles.title: Beyond Korogocho and Viwandani: Sampling Bias and External Validity in Research on Single Motherhood in Nairobi, Kenya
articles.abstract: Empirical research on single motherhood in Nairobi, Kenya relies heavily on cohorts nested inside two informal settlements, Korogocho and Viwandani, monitored by the Nairobi Urban Health and Demographic Surveillance System (NUHDSS). Although these two sites house an estimated 80,000 to 85,000 residents, representing less than 2% of Nairobi County's 4,397,073 population, findings from their cohorts frequently stand in for urban single motherhood across Kenya. This critical literature review audits 10 major empirical studies, national Demographic and Health Survey (KDHS) analyses (2008 to 2022), and official demographic reports to assess the external validity of Nairobi's single-motherhood evidence base. Three core findings emerge. First, severe socio-economic divergence separates NUHDSS samples from Nairobi's wider urban population: 86.3% of mothers in the Jamaa na Afya ya Mtoto (JAMO) cohort lack regular salaried jobs and only 14.9% of Korogocho single mothers completed secondary school, whereas 2022 KDHS data show 43% nonmarital fertility in Nairobi, 31% urban female household headship, and a rise in higher education among never-married Kenyan women from 9.5% to 21.7%. Second, scarce evidence from formal mixed-income estates such as Zimmerman in Roysambu shows distinct care models, with 41.2% of single mothers relying on paid domestic workers rather than informal slum daycares or rural fostering. Third, informal-settlement sampling bias persists because of surveillance infrastructure economics and an unmapped split between Kenya's 11 census sub-counties and 17 electoral constituencies. The paper concludes with a cross-stratum analytical framework and concrete multi-channel sampling strategies for urban family research outside HDSS boundaries.

articles.title: Federalism and Loosely Coupled Intelligent Centers: Practical Insights for the Implementation of AI in the Public Sector in Switzerland

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: In Switzerland, the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in government follows the existing division of powers. The cantons develop AI applications in the fields they run, such as policing and education, while the federal government in its own domains, such as defense and technology. Rather than building a single “intelligent center”, federal systems should therefore govern AI through loosely coupled intelligent centers. This means combining a layer of binding national standards for data security, data access and interfaces, with sectoral and regional hubs that build on existing intergovernmental bodies, pool costs, and leave room for subnational autonomy.

articles.title: Whose Predictions to Trust? The Limits of Expertise and the Promise of Techniques
articles.abstract: After major events, such as the Russian invasion of Ukraine, there are always some scholars whose predictions appear to have been more accurate. Yet it is hard to know whether their success reflects genuine skill or mere luck. This paper examines why some individuals are consistently better at predicting events in international relations months and years ahead. Drawing on 435,000 forecasts from 924 scholars, officers, analysts, and amateurs on political and military events between 2017 and 2026, we develop a joint model of individual forecasting accuracy and analyze the relative importance of techniques, expertise, and psychological traits. We find that traditional criteria, such as subject-matter expertise and seniority, are poor predictors of accuracy. While cognitive traits, especially fluid intelligence, matter more, the techniques individuals use are stronger predictors of longer-term accuracy. We identify three common forecasting approaches: intuitive, theoretical-historical, and probabilistic. While fast, intuitive (System 1) thinking appears to reduce accuracy, not all forms of slower (System 2) thinking help. Drawing on theories and historical analogies appears to have little effect, whereas probabilistic reasoning strongly predicts higher accuracy. These findings call for a clearer distinction between identifying which future events may occur, where subject-matter expertise is essential, and assessing their likelihood, where other skills are required.

articles.title: The (In)formation of a Knowing State: The 1927 Census and the Making of a Public Information Infrastructure in Turkey
articles.abstract: Within fifteen years the early Turkish Republic set up a statistical office and ran a general population census. It also rebuilt its postal and telegraph administration, opened a broadcasting service and legislated on population and property records. The literature usually tells these as separate institutional histories. This study reads them together, as three layers of one public information infrastructure: collection, transmission and storage. It asks how law and administrative practice linked the layers between 1923 and 1938, and what the record shows of their use. It analyses published primary sources: sixteen statutes of the period from the Grand National Assembly's statute book, fourteen read for content and two for chronology only. Five later statutes, the Population Law of 1914 and the official publication of the 1927 census, which prints its methods, laws, instructions, schedule and analysis, complete the corpus. Secondary studies fill gaps in this record. The sources read show four information relations between the layers, at different levels of evidence. The law of 1927 on building numbers provided for handing the schedules to the population, land registry, tax and municipal offices and cadastral teams. On paper, this gave five record systems one address frame. The census schedule contained questions on whether each person was already in the population registers and held an identity card. No comparison of the answers with the registers is documented. The statistics law of 1930 had the vital statistics compiled with the help of the population offices. The census volume reports the telegraph carrying the returns. The census can be described as an information workflow, with a pilot stage, an address frame, field control, cross-checked totals and 8,632,000 punched cards tabulated by machine. The instruments provide for publication and reporting, but the primary record does not document the link the literature draws between two decisions and the 1927 results. These arrangements show how the production, transmission and storage of public information were organised. Today's questions about standards, shared identifiers, data quality and confidentiality can be put to them. The record shows a state learning to know more clearly than a state using what it knew.

articles.title: Camp Andalusia Revisited: Tracing of the Internment of German Civilians in South Africa during the WWII
articles.authors: Jan Hasil, Garth Benneyworth, Shawn Berry, Ladislav Damašek, Petr Hasil, Václav Čáp Podhrázský
articles.abstract: Camp Andalusia, near Jan Kempdorp in the Northern Cape, held German male civilians from South West Africa, from other British-administered territories of Africa and from captured merchant vessels between 1940 and 1945. Knowledge of the camp has so far rested on written sources, memoirs and period plans that are not tied to the topography. In 2026 the camp was relocated and its surface remains were documented by UAV-based and terrestrial photogrammetry and RTK-GNSS survey. The resulting orthophotos, three-dimensional models and georeferenced catalogue cover approximately two fifths of the camp area. Selected features were excavated and documented in detail: the swimming pool, a building of uncertain function (‘lavatory’), two types of accommodation bungalows and informal structures, namely the gardens created by the internees.

articles.title: Who Can Decline a Turn? Chess, Zugzwang, and Europe’s Empty Chair Crisis
articles.abstract: This paper uses two king-and-pawn positions to examine how the obligation to move can affect an endgame’s outcome. It then considers France’s 1965 boycott of European Economic Community Council meetings and the Luxembourg Compromise. The paper argues that the leverage of nonparticipation depends on which decisions others can take independently, what they need to decide together, and who bears the costs of waiting. Working Paper 07 in Who Gets to Move? Chess and the Politics of Possibility.

articles.title: Beyond a Single Continuum: Multidimensional Gender Ideology and Task-Specific Housework Sharing across 29 Countries
articles.abstract: Support for gender equality has grown, yet routine housework remains largely women's work. This study asks whether people with different combinations of gender beliefs share different household tasks, and whether the kind of task shared matters for perceived fairness and wellbeing. We use the 2022 International Social Survey Programme for partnered adults in 29 countries. Latent class analysis of ten attitude items identifies five ideology profiles: egalitarian (35%), egalitarian essentialist (19%), ambivalent (18%), homemaking-valuing (10%) and traditional (18%). Country-specific regressions are pooled by random-effects meta-analysis. Egalitarians share more tasks than every other profile, and the difference is largest for laundry, cleaning and cooking. Egalitarian essentialists, who support maternal employment but regard daily childcare as the mother's job, share shopping and family activities almost as often as egalitarians but share routine chores much less. Reports of a fair division rise more steeply with the sharing of routine chores than with the sharing of flexible tasks, by 30 percentage points among women and 30 among men. Egalitarian profiles are more common where national gender inequality is lower. Equality in routine chores is what separates egalitarian households from others, and it is the standard partners use to judge fairness.
